newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia in opening bid for coal price rise.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia in opening bid for coal price rise.

text.p: Australia has made an opening gambit in 1997/98 coal price negotiations with Japan in requesting a price rise of about 10 percent for hard coking coal, double the increase negotiated for 1996/97.

Australian producers said on Thursday that market conditions and currency movements created conditions for a further rise in price following the five percent increase negotiated for Japanese fiscal 1996/97 ending March 31.

Japanese trade publications say Australian producers presented the Japanese steel mills with a price rise request of US$6.00 a tonne after the recent Australia-Japan business cooperation meetings in Sydney.
Australian coal industry executives contacted by Reuters said the increase would compensate for the strengthening Australian dollar and take account of tight supplies.
Since late last year when the latest Australia-Japan coking coal price was set, the Australian dollar has risen to about US$0.79 from $0.73, a gain of more than eight percent.
"Historically the exchange rate is something that everybody knows about but which is kept in the background," one coal executive said.
Australia's coal exports to Japan, the leading market, are priced in US dollars and a strengthening Australian dollar reduces returns to the Australian producers.

"The exchange rate is a fact. There is no doubt that Australian producers will be looking at the A$ return and I think it's timely to remind the Japanese that it is a factor," said an Australian producer, who asked not to be named.
Declines in both Australia's negotiated coal export prices and the Australian dollar over the past two decades showed some recognition of a relationship between price and currency, he said.
"I think that's certainly the feeling for hard coking coal that there will be a price rise for the coming year," he said.

Australia's weather also loomed as a potential major factor on the supply side, he said, pointing to forecast rain for the coming summer, notably the monsoon rains in the major coking coal province of central Queensland.
"A few flooded pits and the whole supply situation will get a lot tighter," he said.
This would add to the present tight market for hard coking coal, he said. "It's very finely balanced," he said.
Other Australian producers said that while no specific prices had been placed on the table, Australia would be pressing for further price rises in the coming negotiating season.

Early this year, Australian producers, led by The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, negotiated an average price rise for hard coking coal of about five percent, bringing the benchmark price to about $54.50 a tonne.
A $6 a tonne price rise would represent a gain of more than 10 percent and boost the hard coking coal price to above $60.00 a tonne.

Australia exported about 139 million tonnes of coal in 1995/96 ended June 30, with about 76 million tonnes of that coking coal. Australia is the world's largest coal exporter and coal the country's biggest export.
